notes.meaning: God commands Ezekiel to sing a lament, which is a mournful funeral song, for the royal leaders of Judah. In the ancient world, people sang laments only after someone had died, but here God pronounces the death of the royal family before it fully happens. This showed the people that the downfall of their rulers was certain because of their sins.

Ezekiel compares the nation of Judah to a mother lioness resting among the pagan nations. Instead of living as God's holy and separate people, Judah copied the violent and greedy ways of the kingdoms around her. She raised her young royal sons with these worldly habits rather than teaching them to follow the Lord.

The mother lioness trained one of her cubs until he grew up to be a fierce predator. This points to King Jehoahaz, the son of good King Josiah, who quickly showed a cruel and greedy spirit once he took the throne. He used his royal power to harm and mistreat the very people he was meant to protect.

The surrounding nations heard about his violent rule, and Pharaoh Necho of Egypt marched against him. The Egyptians trapped him like a wild animal in a hidden pit and dragged him away with hooks to Egypt. Jehoahaz was removed after reigning only three months and died as a captive in a foreign land.

Judah waited for some time, hoping that Jehoahaz might return from captivity, but that hope soon vanished. So the nation took another of Josiah's sons, Jehoiakim, and placed him on the throne. They foolishly believed that a new king using the same worldly methods would restore their power.

Jehoiakim walked among the violent rulers of the surrounding world and became just as fierce as they were. During his eleven years as king, he oppressed the innocent, stole from his subjects, and defied the Lord. He copied the cruel ways of pagan empires instead of following God's law of justice.

This ruler attacked the estates of wealthy citizens, tearing down their strongholds and leaving cities deserted. The entire land and its people lived in terror whenever this cruel king shouted his threats. God sees and remembers when earthly leaders abuse their authority to terrorize others.

Babylon and armies from the surrounding provinces came together against Jehoiakim to put down his rebellion. Like hunters surrounding a dangerous beast, they closed in on him from every side and caught him in their net. Human strength cannot stand when God brings judgment upon wicked rulers.

The conquerors locked the king in a cage with hooks and marched him away to the king of Babylon. This brought a complete end to his arrogant threats across the mountains of Israel. Earthly pride and boasting always come to an end before God's righteous judgment.

The song turns to a second picture, describing Judah as a healthy vine planted beside rich streams of water. Under God's blessings and covenant care, Israel had enjoyed peace, safety, and a large population. God gives people every opportunity to thrive and bear good fruit.

The vine grew strong, sturdy branches that were fit to be royal scepters, which are ornamental rods held by rulers. The royal line of David rose to great fame, standing tall and proud above all the nations around it. God blessed this kingdom with honor, yet its leaders grew proud of their position.

Because of Judah's rebellion and sin, God tore the vine up by its roots and threw it to the ground in anger. The Babylonian army swept in like a dry, scorching east wind from the desert, withering the nation's fruit. The royal line was broken and consumed in the fire of national ruin.

The uprooted vine was then transplanted far away into the dry, thirsty desert of Babylon. Even though Babylon had plenty of natural rivers, it was a harsh wasteland for the captive Jews who were stripped of their temple and freedom. Sin can carry people away from places of blessing into dry seasons of exile.

A destructive fire broke out from one of the vine's own branches and burned up what was left of the tree. This points to King Zedekiah, whose rebellion against Babylon brought total destruction on Jerusalem and the temple. The dynasty of David was left without an earthly king to rule on the throne, ending the song in deep mourning.
